messages.content: Why are the dot products in scaled dot-product attention divided by the square root of d_k?

For large key dimensions the dot products grow in magnitude, which pushes the softmax into regions where its gradients are extremely small. Dividing by sqrt(d_k) keeps the scores in a moderate range so the softmax stays well-behaved and training remains stable.
What are the two sub-layers in each Transformer encoder layer?

Each encoder layer has a multi-head self-attention sub-layer followed by a position-wise fully connected feed-forward sub-layer. Each sub-layer is wrapped in a residual connection followed by layer normalization.
What does the position-wise feed-forward network do in a Transformer layer?

It applies the same small two-layer network to every position independently: a linear transformation, a ReLU, and a second linear transformation. It adds non-linear processing after attention has mixed information across positions.
What is encoder-decoder attention in the Transformer?

In this decoder sub-layer the queries come from the previous decoder layer, while the keys and values come from the encoder output. This lets every decoder position attend over all positions of the input sequence, similar to attention in earlier sequence-to-sequence models.
What goes wrong if the decoder's self-attention is not masked during training?

Each position could attend to later target tokens, so the model could simply copy the answer it is supposed to predict instead of learning to predict it. Masking future positions preserves the autoregressive property, so training matches how generation works at inference time.
What is the main computational drawback of self-attention on long sequences?

Self-attention compares every pair of positions, so its time and memory cost grow quadratically with sequence length. This becomes expensive for very long inputs, which motivated later work on restricted or more efficient attention.
What size was the base Transformer model in the original paper?
The base model used 6 encoder layers and 6 decoder layers, a model dimension of 512, 8 attention heads, and a feed-forward inner dimension of 2048.
Why does the Transformer use residual connections around each sub-layer?

A residual connection lets each sub-layer learn a refinement of its input rather than a full transformation, and it gives gradients a direct path through the deep stack. Combined with layer normalization, this makes training many stacked layers stable.
What optimizer and learning-rate schedule did the original Transformer use?

It used the Adam optimizer with a warmup schedule: the learning rate increases linearly for the first warmup steps (4000 in the paper) and then decays in proportion to the inverse square root of the step number.
How did the original Transformer perform on machine translation?
It reached 28.4 BLEU on WMT 2014 English-to-German and a single-model state-of-the-art 41.8 BLEU on English-to-French, at a fraction of the training cost of the previous best models.
Where is dropout applied in the Transformer?

Dropout is applied to the output of each sub-layer before it is added to the residual input and normalized, and also to the sums of the embeddings and positional encodings. The base model used a dropout rate of 0.1.
What do the final linear layer and softmax do in the Transformer decoder?
The decoder's output vectors are passed through a learned linear transformation and a softmax to produce a probability distribution over the vocabulary for the next token.
What do the rank r and the scaling factor alpha control in LoRA?

The rank r is the inner dimension of the two low-rank matrices, so it sets the capacity of the update and the number of trainable parameters. The update is scaled by alpha divided by r, which controls how strongly the adapter changes the pretrained weights.
What observation motivates LoRA?

LoRA builds on the observation that the weight updates needed to adapt a pretrained model to a new task have a low intrinsic rank. If the update is effectively low-rank, it can be represented by the product of two small matrices instead of a full-size update matrix.
How much does LoRA reduce trainable parameters and memory for GPT-3 175B?

Compared with fine-tuning GPT-3 175B with Adam, LoRA can reduce the number of trainable parameters by about 10,000 times and the GPU memory requirement by about 3 times, while performing on par with or better than full fine-tuning in model quality.
What happens if the LoRA rank is set too low?

The adapter has too little capacity to express the weight update the task needs, so the model can underfit, especially on tasks that differ a lot from the pretraining data. The paper found surprisingly small ranks work for many tasks, but a very low rank can still limit quality.
What happens if the LoRA rank is set much higher than needed?

Trainable parameters and memory grow, but quality usually stops improving because the useful update has low intrinsic rank. A higher rank mostly adds cost and a greater risk of overfitting on small datasets without meaningful accuracy gains.
For a weight matrix of size d by k, how many parameters does a LoRA update use?
LoRA represents the update as B times A, where B is d by r and A is r by k, so it trains r times (d plus k) parameters instead of d times k. For small r this is a tiny fraction of the full matrix.
Which models did the LoRA paper evaluate on?
The paper evaluated LoRA on RoBERTa, DeBERTa, GPT-2, and GPT-3 175B, reporting quality on par with or better than full fine-tuning while training far fewer parameters.
What is the difference between RAG-Sequence and RAG-Token?

RAG-Sequence conditions the whole generated output on one retrieved document at a time and marginalizes over the retrieved documents for the full sequence. RAG-Token lets each generated token be conditioned on a possibly different document, marginalizing at every token step.
What retriever and generator did the original RAG model use?
The original RAG model paired a Dense Passage Retriever, a bi-encoder using maximum inner product search over a dense index of Wikipedia passages, with a BART sequence-to-sequence generator.
What are the parametric and non-parametric memories in RAG?

The parametric memory is the pretrained sequence-to-sequence generator, whose knowledge is stored in its weights. The non-parametric memory is the dense vector index of Wikipedia passages that the retriever searches.
Which components of RAG are trained jointly, and which are kept fixed?

The generator and the query encoder of the retriever are fine-tuned together end to end. The document encoder and the pre-built document index are kept fixed, which avoids re-indexing the corpus during training.
What happens when a RAG retriever returns irrelevant passages?

The generator receives misleading or off-topic context, so it may produce a wrong or unrelated answer, or it may fall back on its own parametric knowledge. The quality of the final answer is bounded by the quality of retrieval.
What kinds of tasks was RAG evaluated on?
RAG was evaluated on open-domain question answering such as Natural Questions and TriviaQA, abstractive question answering, Jeopardy question generation, and fact verification with FEVER.
In the RAG paper, how did dense retrieval compare with BM25?

A learned dense retriever outperformed a BM25 baseline on most tasks, such as open-domain question answering. On fact verification (FEVER) BM25 did better, which the authors attributed to claims being entity-heavy and suited to word-overlap matching.
What loss is used to train a prototypical network?

The loss is the negative log-probability of the true class for each query point, where the class probabilities come from a softmax over negative distances to the class prototypes. It is minimized by gradient descent over many sampled episodes.
Does a prototypical network need the same number of classes per training episode as at test time?
No. The paper found that training with a higher number of classes per episode than will be used at test time can improve performance, so matching the training and test way is not required.
What kind of network produces the embeddings in a prototypical network?

A neural encoder, such as a convolutional network for images, maps each input into an embedding space. It is trained so that examples of the same class cluster around their class prototype and stay far from the prototypes of other classes.
How can prototypical networks be extended to zero-shot learning?

Instead of averaging support examples, the prototype for each class is produced by embedding class meta-data, such as attribute vectors, with a separate encoder. Queries are then classified by their distance to these meta-data prototypes.
On which benchmarks were prototypical networks evaluated?
The paper evaluated few-shot classification on Omniglot and miniImageNet, and showed a zero-shot extension on the Caltech-UCSD Birds (CUB-200) dataset.
What are full context embeddings in Matching Networks?

Full context embeddings make each support example's embedding depend on the whole support set, using a bidirectional LSTM, and refine the query embedding with an attention LSTM that reads the support set. This makes embeddings context-aware instead of embedding every example independently.
What attention kernel do Matching Networks use to compare a query with the support examples?
They use a softmax over the cosine distance between the query embedding and each support embedding. The resulting attention weights form a weighted vote over the support labels.
How do Matching Networks relate to nearest-neighbor methods?

They can be seen as a differentiable, learned form of nearest-neighbor or kernel-based classification: the prediction is a weighted combination of the support labels, with the weights coming from an attention kernel over learned embeddings.
What datasets were Matching Networks evaluated on?
Matching Networks were evaluated on Omniglot, on one-shot tasks built from ImageNet, where the paper introduced miniImageNet as a benchmark, and on one-shot language modeling with Penn Treebank.
What calibration data does GPTQ need?

GPTQ needs only a small calibration set of text samples, such as a few hundred random segments of a few thousand tokens, to estimate second-order information for each layer. It needs no labels and no retraining.
How long does GPTQ take to quantize very large models?
The paper reports that GPTQ can quantize GPT-style models with 175 billion parameters in approximately four GPU hours.
What bit widths does GPTQ target?

GPTQ mainly quantizes weights to 3 or 4 bits per weight, with some experiments at 2 bits or ternary levels, while keeping accuracy close to the full-precision model for large LLMs. Activations are typically kept in higher precision.
How does GPTQ accuracy change as the bit width gets very low?
Accuracy is usually close to full precision at 4 bits, shows a modest loss at 3 bits, and degrades sharply at 2 bits or ternary levels unless extra tricks such as grouping are used.
Which model families was GPTQ evaluated on?
GPTQ was evaluated on large open language models from the OPT and BLOOM families, reporting perplexity and zero-shot accuracy at 3 and 4 bits.
How are SmoothQuant's smoothing factors applied without adding inference cost?

The per-channel scaling factors are folded offline into the preceding operation, such as the parameters of the previous LayerNorm, and into the weights. Because the equivalent transformation is absorbed into existing parameters, no extra scaling operations are needed at inference time.
What goes wrong if SmoothQuant's migration strength alpha is too large?

Too much quantization difficulty is shifted from the activations to the weights, so the weights develop outliers and become hard to quantize, and accuracy drops. If alpha is too small, the activation outliers remain and activation quantization stays difficult.
Where do the hard-to-quantize outliers appear in LLM activations?

They appear in a few specific channels with very large magnitudes that are consistent across tokens, while the weights are comparatively flat. A single per-tensor scale for the activations is then dominated by these outliers, wasting precision for all the other channels.
Which models was SmoothQuant demonstrated on?
SmoothQuant was demonstrated on a wide range of LLM families, including OPT, BLOOM, GLM, and the 530B-parameter MT-NLG, and later on Llama, Falcon, and Mistral models.
How is the distillation loss typically formed?

It is a weighted combination of two terms: a soft-target term, the cross-entropy between the student's and the teacher's temperature-softened distributions, and a hard-label term, the usual cross-entropy with the true labels.
Can distillation compress an ensemble into a single model?
Yes. The paper shows that the knowledge of an ensemble can be distilled into a single model, keeping much of the ensemble's accuracy gain while being far cheaper to deploy.
Why can a student trained on soft targets learn from less data?

Soft targets carry much more information per training example than hard labels and have less variance in the gradient between examples. In the paper's speech experiment, a model trained on only a small fraction of the data with soft targets nearly matched one trained on all of it.
What experiments did Hinton and colleagues use to evaluate distillation?

The paper reports experiments on MNIST, on an acoustic model for speech recognition, and on specialist models for a very large image dataset, showing that distilled models retain much of the benefit of an ensemble.
How do GPTQ and SmoothQuant differ in what they quantize?

GPTQ is a weight-only method that rounds weights using second-order error compensation and keeps activations in higher precision. SmoothQuant targets quantizing both weights and activations to 8 bits by rescaling channels to move activation outliers into the weights.
How does knowledge distillation differ from quantization as a way of compressing a model?

Distillation trains a new, smaller model to imitate a larger model's outputs, so the architecture itself shrinks. Quantization keeps the architecture but stores weights, and sometimes activations, at lower precision. The two can be combined.
How does LoRA differ from quantization in reducing the cost of working with LLMs?

LoRA reduces the cost of training by updating only small low-rank matrices on top of frozen weights, while quantization reduces the memory and compute needed to store and run the weights at lower precision. They address different costs and can be combined.
Why is retrieval a useful complement to a fine-tuned small language model?

A small model cannot memorize many facts in its weights, but retrieval can supply the relevant passages at inference time. Fine-tuning can then teach the model how to use that context and to answer in the desired concise style.
Why are prototypical networks attractive for personalizing a model to a new user from a handful of examples?

A new user's class prototypes can be computed by averaging the embeddings of a few enrollment examples, with no gradient update to the network. The prototypes are cheap to store and update, which suits on-device personalization.
